sections.title: Form and structure
sections.text: Sparassis crispa (Wulfen) Fr., the cauliflower fungus, forms a large rounded fruitbody, usually 10–25 cm tall and up to about 40 cm wide. Numerous flattened, wavy and frilled ribbons arise from a thick central base, often buried and connected to roots. The smooth fertile surface covers the lobes: this species has no cap, ordinary aerial stem, gills or pores.

sections.title: Colour and flesh
sections.text: The lobes are whitish to cream or pale yellow, sometimes tinged with ochre or pink; they brown and become tougher with age. Young flesh is pliable, firm and somewhat cartilaginous. The spore print is off-white. A cut through the centre shows pale tissue arranged in flattened branches, without tubes or a hollow centre.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This species grows at the base of, or on the roots of, conifers, especially pine and more rarely other conifers depending on region. It causes brown root and butt rot and may fruit at the same location for several years. Fruiting bodies appear mainly from late summer into autumn.

sections.title: Look-alikes and caution
sections.text: Other Sparassis species, including S. brevipes, are close and their distinction may depend on habitat, fine characters and region; a photograph alone may not settle the identification. Ramaria and other coral fungi have more cylindrical branches, unlike the broad frilled ribbons of S. crispa. DGfM and VAPKO lists include it among edible species, but those lists never confirm the identity of a find. Do not eat an uncertain specimen.

traits: Large rounded fruitbody of flattened, frilled ribbons, up to about 40 cm wide, arising from a central base
Lobes whitish to cream or pale yellow, browning and toughening with age
Smooth fertile surface on the lobes · no gills or pores · off-white spore print
Young flesh pliable, firm and somewhat cartilaginous; base often connected to roots
At the base of or on conifer roots, especially pine; mainly late summer to autumn
safetyNote: DGfM and VAPKO lists include Sparassis crispa among edible species; this does not confirm the identity of a specimen. The lobes readily trap debris, and older fruitbodies become tough. Do not eat a mushroom identified only from this page or a photograph; if uncertain, ask a qualified mycologist or mushroom inspector.
